title: Tecumseh falls at the Thames, Oct. 5, 1813
summary: Tecumseh was killed at the Thames in Ontario on Oct. 5, 1813, when Isaac Shelby's Kentucky volunteers broke the British line and his confederacy collapsed.
bodyMarkdown:
Kentucky’s long frontier fight with the Shawnee-led confederacy ended far from home, on the Thames River in what is now southwestern Ontario. After Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry’s American squadron won control of [Lake Erie](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Lake_Erie) on September 10, 1813, British Major General Henry Procter burned Fort Malden and Detroit and retreated east along the Thames. Governor [Isaac Shelby](/people/#isaac-shelby), then sixty-three and a veteran of Kings Mountain in the Revolution, answered William Henry Harrison’s call by raising more than 3,500 Kentucky volunteers, mostly mounted riflemen, and led them north in person.

The Kentuckians were still angry about the [River Raisin](/stories/river-raisin-1813-kentuckys-winter-defeat-in-michigan/) the previous January, where hundreds of their neighbors had been killed or captured. “Remember the Raisin!” had become a statewide rallying cry. Shelby’s brigades joined Harrison’s Army of the Northwest and pushed hard after Procter’s column, which was slowed by wagons, baggage, and a thin supply of ammunition.

On October 5, 1813, near Moraviantown, Procter formed about 800 British regulars and militia in a thin line along a road pinched by swamp. Roughly 500 warriors of Tecumseh’s confederacy, including Shawnee, Wyandot, and others, held the wooded marsh beside them. Harrison put Shelby’s infantry opposite the British and sent Col. [Richard M. Johnson](/people/#richard-m-johnson)’s Kentucky mounted regiment to the right, into the swamp.

Johnson’s horsemen charged through the wet ground. One battalion broke the British square in minutes; Procter fled, and hundreds of his men surrendered. The other battalion closed with the Native line. In that fight [Tecumseh](/people/#tecumseh) was killed. Who fired the fatal shot was never settled—Johnson later claimed it, and so did other Kentuckians—but the Shawnee leader’s death was confirmed on the field. His warriors broke and scattered when word of it spread.

Tecumseh, born about 1768, had spent years trying to unite the nations of the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes against further American land cessions. After Tippecanoe and the early British successes of 1812, his alliance was the last organized Native force that could threaten Kentucky’s northern border. With him gone, the confederacy collapsed. Tribes that had fought beside him sued for peace; British power west of Lake Erie never recovered.

For Kentucky the Thames closed a generation of raids and winter campaigns that had reached from the Bluegrass to the Detroit River. Shelby brought most of his volunteers home. Johnson’s wounds and reputation carried him into national politics. The northern shore of the Ohio was, for the first time since statehood, beyond the reach of a coordinated Native-British war.

## Kentucky today

The battlefield lies in Chatham-Kent, Ontario, near the Thames. Kentucky remembers the campaign in county names for officers lost at the River Raisin and in the state marker “Remember the Raisin” on the Scott County courthouse lawn in Georgetown, where many of the volunteers mustered. Shelby’s second governorship and the mounted charge at the Thames remain the commonwealth’s clearest War of 1812 story.
